---
title: "Case study: Sunshine Canyon, Colorado"
description: "A 115 kV line in the wildland-urban interface, where the LiDAR barely sampled the conductor."
---

| | |
|---|---|
| Line | Sunshine–Boulder Hydro 115 kV, wood H-frames (OSM way 1381464850) |
| Setting | Wildland–urban interface west of Boulder; the 2010 Fourmile Canyon Fire burned about 2.5 km away |
| LiDAR | `CO_DRCOG_2020`, flown 29 May 2020 (14:25 to 14:50 UTC, from the point GPS times), UTM metres, ~35 pts/m², ground / unclassified / noise only |
| Line length, above-ground points | 1.52 km, 2.26 M |
| Conductor returns found | 914, along 2% of the line |
| Result | Bounded: 3 robust grow-in candidates, 27 segments undecidable |

![Sunshine risk map](../reference/figures/sunshine_risk_map.png)

## The conductor is barely sampled

![Sunshine conductor profile](../reference/figures/sunshine_conductor_profile.png)

After the sanity checks, conductor returns survive along 2% of the line, and spans run 257–468 m between H-frames across a 250 m descent into the canyon. Along 22% of the line the next support is outside the data, so there is no upper bound at all.

| | optimistic conductor (upper bound) | pessimistic conductor (code minimum) |
|---|---|---|
| segments with ≥ 5 m² of canopy inside the clearance target | **3 of 30** | 30 of 30 |
| potential strike trees | 14 | 135 |

Clearance is radial: the 3D distance from the canopy column to the outer phase, scored out to 14 m either side of the centreline (the conductor returns reach 13.5 m). Strike trees stand beyond that zone; the optimistic count takes trees that reach the conductor at every plausible elevation inside its bracket, the pessimistic count those that reach it at some plausible elevation. Supports for the upper bound are the 5 tagged H-frames; the 9 other vertices of the OSM way are bends, not structures.

- **3 robust grow-in candidates.** The top one (about 1.01–1.06 km along the line, conductor measured along 41% of it) has a conductor about 15 m up, leaving a low H-frame on the canyon floor, beside riparian cottonwoods up to 27 m tall. The other two have trees of 20–29 m that exceed even the highest plausible conductor. They are the places to verify with imagery or a field visit first.
- **27 segments are bound-dependent.** Whether they need work depends on where the conductor actually is, which this acquisition doesn't show.
- **The LiDAR saw the corridor.** Every segment has at least 94% of its corridor and 88% of its grow-in zone observed (median 100%), so none is tiered `no data`. Five stations have an H-frame's 8 m mask inside their grow-in zone; it covers at most 17% of it.

## By span

The OSM way is 3.2 km long and carries 14 vertices, 5 of them tagged H-frames; the study window is the 1.52 km the LiDAR covers. Rolled up to structure-to-structure spans:

| span | length | stations | optimistic tier | pessimistic tier | strike trees, some / every plausible height |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|
| S12789370510 > S3704238536 | 63 m | 1 | none | grow-in | 2 / 0 |
| S3704238536 > S3704238218 | 401 m | 8 | **grow-in** | grow-in | 34 / 4 |
| S3704238218 > S4297189776 | 315 m | 6 | none | grow-in | 17 / 0 |
| S4297189776 > S4297189775 | 468 m | 9 | **grow-in** | grow-in | 56 / 10 |

Every span is bound-dependent; 109 of the 135 possible strike trees and all 14 certain ones stand in a span. Six of the 30 stations lie before the first or after the last tagged structure inside the data and belong to no span; the upper conductor bound is unknown there anyway. Span ids are the OSM node ids of the end structures, so they survive a re-run, a new LiDAR epoch and a different CRS.

## Wires do not generalise across space here

| class | n | prevalence | avg. precision, spatial blocks | random folds | spatial, no height/echo |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| building | 3,608 | 0.0016 | 0.54 | 0.82 | 0.60 |
| structure | 1,602 | 0.0007 | 0.052 | 0.45 | 0.012 |
| wire | 914 | 0.0004 | 0.009 | 0.20 | 0.014 |

![Sunshine cross-validation](../reference/figures/sunshine_cv_metrics.png)

With only a few hundred metres of labelled conductor and five structures, wires and structures don't generalise across space. Random folds would have hidden that: they report a wire average precision of 0.20 where spatial blocks report 0.009.

The pooled spatial figure rests on very little, so it is reported fold by fold as well. The 914 wire points sit in four 100 m blocks, and one block holds 697 of them (76%): however the blocks are dealt, one fold holds most of the class and one holds none. Blocks are dealt to folds by class presence, which puts the four in four different folds, and wire average precision by fold is 0.005, 0.016, 0.039 and 0.13 (median 0.028). Each is far below the random-fold 0.20, so the direction of the gap is not in doubt; its size is known to an order of magnitude, no better. Structures (four scored folds, 0.03 to 0.29) and buildings (three, 0.52 to 0.94) are in the same position.

![Sunshine cross-section](../reference/figures/sunshine_cross_section.png)

## The grown-in canopy is not the dry canopy

A dry-season (July–September) median of 25 Landsat 8 scenes from 2019–2021, bracketing the 2020 flight, covers the corridor with 262 pixels. Only 73 are scored: 85 are under half canopy, and 104, mostly along the corridor edge and inside the bend, are less than 80% observed by the LiDAR, so their reflectance would describe land outside the clip. 22 of the 30 segments rest on at least two scored pixels and 5 m² of grown-in canopy and get a percentile; the others keep their index but aren't ranked. NDVI and NDMI agree closely across the ranked segments (r = 0.92).

| robust grow-in candidate | NDVI percentile | NDMI percentile |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0.10–0.15 km, trees to 20 m | 0.48 | 0.59 |
| 1.01–1.06 km, riparian cottonwoods on the canyon floor (top candidate) | 0.47 | 0.81 |
| 1.06–1.11 km, canyon floor, trees to 29 m | 0.93 | 0.96 |

- **None of the three grow-in candidates is dry.** Two sit in the middle of the corridor's greenness (47th and 48th percentile), and the 1.06–1.11 km segment is among the greenest and wettest canopy on the line (riparian trees on the canyon floor). The top candidate at 1.01–1.06 km is middling by greenness but among the wettest by NDMI, which is what riparian cottonwoods look like from orbit.
- **The 4 driest segments** (lowest NDVI quarter: 0.05–0.10, 0.46–0.51, 0.81–0.86 and 1.22–1.27 km) are all bound-dependent: grow-in only if the conductor is at the code minimum. If the conductor turns out to be low there, encroachment and dry fuel coincide, so these come first among the 27 undecidable segments.

![Sunshine canopy dryness](../reference/figures/sunshine_canopy_dryness.png)

## Fire-weather winds come from one direction, and that splits the strike trees in two

Over 2017–2024 there were 447 fire-weather hours (gusts ≥ 16.5 m/s, RH ≤ 30%) in about 100 distinct events (hours separated by less than six hours count as one); 69% of the hours and half of the events fell in October–December. 98% of the hours came from the west: the Front Range downslope winds behind the 2021 Marshall Fire. The line runs south-west to north-east, so those winds blow trees west of it towards the conductors and trees east of it away.

The wind record is ECMWF IFS at 9 km from the Open-Meteo archive, one product for all eight years. Earlier versions of this page used 2015–2024 with the archive's default product and reported a 15.2 m/s threshold. That record turned out to be two products, ERA5 (25 km) for 2015–2016 and IFS from 2017, identical to the hour with each, and its 95th-percentile gust steps from about 10.5 to about 17 m/s at the change. ERA5 alone would cover more years, but it flattens exactly these windstorms: its strongest gust in the ten years is 32 m/s against 43 m/s in IFS, only 75% of its fire-weather hours come from the west, and they peak in April.

| | strike trees | windward (≥ 50% of fire-weather hours) | wind-weighted strike-tree count |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| pessimistic: conductor at its lower bound | 131 | 48 | 45 |
| optimistic: conductor at its upper bound | 14 | 9 | 8 |

The wind-weighted count is the sum over strike trees of the share of fire-weather hours that would throw each one into the line: how many trees a typical fire-weather hour's winds point at the conductors, *if they fell*. It carries no failure probability. The wind columns are worked out at the two conductor bounds; the 4 further trees that strike only at a conductor height between the bounds (135 in all) are not in them.

- **The split is close to all-or-nothing.** Windward trees are hit in 88% of fire-weather hours on average; the median leeward tree is hit in under 1%.
- **The top grow-in candidate also has the most windward strike trees:** 6 of its 9 that strike at the upper conductor bound, at 1.01–1.06 km. It is the segment to verify first on both counts.
- **The four dry segments** (0.05–0.10, 0.46–0.51, 0.81–0.86 and 1.22–1.27 km) have 5, 2, 1 and 1 potential strike trees, of which 0, 1, 0 and 1 are windward.

![Sunshine wind exposure](../reference/figures/sunshine_wind_exposure.png)

## Configuration

```r
run_case_study(list(
  id = "sunshine",
  line_ids = "1381464850", osm_date = "2026-10-19T14:01:07Z", project = "CO_DRCOG_2020",
  tiles = sprintf("USGS_LPC_CO_DRCOG_2020_B20_%s.laz", c("w0472n4429", "w0472n4430")),
  half_width_m = 45, wire_search_m = 12, phase_offset_m = 5.5,
  under_line_m = 14, wire_zone_m = 15, structure_mask_m = 8,
  min_ground_clear_m = 4.9,            # NESC 232-1, 115 kV, pedestrian-only land
  attach_m = 20,                       # upper limit on wood H-frame attachment height
  vendor_classes = FALSE,
  landsat = list(years = 2019:2021, months = 7:9, dry_index = "ndvi"),
  wind = list(start = "2017-01-01", end = "2024-12-31", model = "ecmwf_ifs",
              gust_quantile = 0.95, max_rh = 30)
))
```

The full script is `analysis/run_sunshine_canyon.R`.
